title: Advance: challenge the centre immediately
caption: After 5...Bxc5: the c-pawn has been exchanged for White's d-pawn. Develop and pressure e5; this is not the ...Bf5 structure.

comments.6: Eric also plays 3...Bf5 in this run. Here ...c5 immediately challenges d4.
comments.8: Recover the pawn through development; do not confuse this position with a Slav pawn grab.
comments.10: The bishop recovers c5. Black now has the d-pawn; White no longer does.

title: Advance: bishop outside the pawn chain
caption: After 8...Nc6: pressure d4 with the c5-pawn and knight. The g8-knight still needs a route that respects e5.

comments.6: Develop the light-squared bishop before closing its diagonal with ...e6.
comments.10: The ...c5 break attacks the base of White's pawn chain.
comments.12: Keeping the bishop invites Bxg6 hxg6, opening the h-file. It is a structural choice, not a forced attack.

title: Early Nf3: the ...Bg4 route
caption: After 8...Nf5: the knight has used e7 because e5 controls f6. Both knights bear on d4.

comments.6: With a white knight on f3, Eric uses ...Bg4 before ...e6.
comments.12: The c-pawn has left c6; the b8-knight can now use that square.
comments.16: An example of ...Nge7-f5. Check g4 and the bishop's retreat squares before copying it.

title: Advance h4: give the bishop a retreat
caption: After 4...h6: h7 is available if the bishop retreats through g6. White can still expand; this move is not a ban on g4.

comments.8: A retreat-square move against h4. Do not close the diagonal with ...e6 without checking g4 and h5.

title: Advance c4: occupy d5 with a piece
caption: After 12...Ned5: ...dxc4 and ...Nb6 cleared d5 for the e7-knight. The remaining d4-pawn is a potential target.

comments.16: By exchanging the d5-pawn, Black creates a d5-square for a piece.
comments.18: ...Nb6 gains time against the bishop and supports d5.
comments.24: The e7-knight reaches d5. This is a plan from this specific pawn structure, not a compulsory sequence.

title: Exchange with Nc3: active bishops and the c-file
caption: After 11...Rc8: c6 has become available for the knight and the c-file is half-open. ...Na5-c4 is a possible later route.

comments.6: Recapture with the c-pawn: c6 becomes a knight square and the c-file becomes half-open.
comments.10: No knight on f3 to pin yet, so the bishop develops to f5.
comments.16: With the f8-bishop already on d6, ...Nge7 does not block it.
comments.18: The recapture improves the knight; doubled pawns are not inevitable after Bxf5.
comments.22: Use the file that actually exists. This game later demonstrates ...Na5-c4.

title: Exchange Bd3 and c3: the fianchetto plan
caption: After 12...e6: the doubled f-pawns help control e4 and the g-file is open. Both kings are castled; king safety still needs calculation.

comments.10: Eric uses ...Qc7 to discourage Bf4 by claiming the c7-f4 diagonal.
comments.16: An alternative to the ...Bd6 setup: develop on g7.
comments.22: This is g7xf5, not e6xf5. The g-file opens and the pawn on f5 controls e4.
comments.24: The structure supports ...Ne4. ...Kh8 and ...Rg8 are possible follow-ups, not automatic moves.

title: Exchange: two pins change development
caption: After 7.Qe2: Nc6 is pinned by Bb5 and the e6-pawn is pinned by Qe2. The study variation uses ...Ne7 instead of Eric's ...Nf6.

comments.13: Black to move. ...Bd6 allows Nxd5: the e6-pawn cannot legally recapture because of Qe2. Eric plays ...Nf6, but Stockfish prefers alternatives including ...Ne7; see the analysis variation.

title: Two Knights: the simple bishop exchange
caption: After 5...e6: Eric has exchanged the g4-bishop for the knight. Black is solid but White owns the bishop pair.

comments.6: ...Bg4 is Eric's recurring response to the Two Knights.
comments.8: The simpler choice against h3: exchange rather than keep a tactically demanding pin.
comments.10: Finish development; giving up the bishop pair is a real concession, not free equality.

title: Two Knights: do not recapture automatically
caption: After 8.Nxc6: the knight attacks Qd8 and the c6-knight is gone. ...Qb6 is the tactical escape; ...bxc6 is the game's mistake.

comments.12: ...Nc6 is playable here. Do not mislabel this developing move as the losing error.
comments.14: The apparent queen sacrifice must be calculated. Stockfish supports accepting it in this exact position.
comments.15: The correction is 8...Qb6. After 8...bxc6 9.Bxc6+ Qd7 10.Bxd7+ Kxd7 11.Kxd1, Black has lost a pawn. Eric explains the ...Qb6 resource in the post-game discussion.

title: Classical: exchange the e4-pawn, develop the bishop
caption: After 13...O-O: Black has completed development. White has space; the next job is to prepare a central break, not sit indefinitely.

comments.6: When White supports e4 with Nc3, ...dxe4 leads to the normal Caro-Kann main lines.
comments.12: Make h7 available for the bishop before h5.
comments.18: Exchange on d3 when the bishop is challenged.
comments.26: A complete short-castled model. The ...c5 arrow is a plan to evaluate, not a forced next move.

title: ...Nd7: develop the c8-bishop later
caption: After 11...c5: Black developed the bishop via b7 and challenged d4. The c6-pawn did not permanently imprison Nb8.

comments.8: The ...Nd7 system delays the c8-bishop. It is a separate branch, not a failure to follow ...Bf5.
comments.12: The e-pawn supports development and guards d5.
comments.20: ...b6 and ...Bb7 solve the remaining bishop problem.
comments.22: The central break arrives after castling and development.

title: ...Nd7: calculate the sacrifice on f7
caption: After 7...Bd6: White can try Nxf7, but Stockfish does not support the sacrifice here. Eric's later loss is not an opening refutation.

comments.14: This developing move is playable. 8.Nxf7 is a speculative sacrifice, not a forced win for White. The analysis variation shows Black accepting and reorganizing.

title: ...Nf6 and ...gxf6: activity for structure
caption: After 7...e6: the f6-pawn controls e5, the g-file is open, and the light-squared bishop is developed. Black must still solve king safety.

comments.8: Eric tries ...Nf6 as well as ...Bf5 and ...Nd7.
comments.10: ...gxf6 accepts doubled f-pawns and opens the g-file. ...exf6 is a different structure; do not combine their plans.
comments.14: Development before exploitation. This is not a license to grab every queenside pawn.

title: Early Bc4: gain a tempo in the centre
caption: After 8...Bd6: ...d5 chased the bishop and Black developed with threats. The bishop on b3 meets a defended d5-pawn.

comments.4: Attack Bc4 while occupying the centre.
comments.6: The pawn recapture supports the centre and clears c6.
comments.12: Develop the bishop before ...e6. Qf3 does not make f7 fall automatically.
comments.16: A possible ...d4 gains time against Nc3, but always check the exact queen and knight squares.

title: Accelerated Panov: activity against the isolated pawn
caption: After 11...Bb7: White has an isolated d4-pawn but active pieces. Black develops first; an isolated pawn is a target, not a forced win.

comments.8: ...Nf6 develops before recovering d5. This avoids an early queen chase.
comments.10: Recover the pawn with a knight.
comments.22: ...b6 and ...Bb7 complete the setup. Contain d4-d5 and compare exchanges carefully.

title: Fantasy: Eric's ...e6 response
caption: After 6...Nh6: ...e6 and ...c5 produced a French-like centre. The knight eyes f5; the light-squared bishop remains inside the chain.

comments.6: A practical response to 3.f3 shown in the run. It allows a French-like structure rather than insisting on an outside bishop.
comments.12: A route to f5. The position also contains ...Qh4+ ideas because f3 weakened that diagonal; they are not universally winning.

title: Quiet d3: take the centre when allowed
caption: After 9...Nbd7: Black has e5 and d5, developed the kingside and castled. ...Re8 supports the centre before further expansion.

comments.6: Against this quiet d3/Nd2 system, Eric takes additional space with ...e5.
comments.18: Because c6 remains occupied by a pawn, the b8-knight develops to d7. Keep the centre defended before pushing farther.

title: Against d4 and c4: a separate Slav branch
caption: After 13...Bb7: ...dxc4 and ...b5 allowed the bishop to develop actively. This is a Semi-Slav structure, not a Caro-Kann.

comments.8: ...e6 before developing Bc8 is legitimate here: pressure on d5 and b7 changes priorities.
comments.20: Only now release the central tension.
comments.26: The bishop joins through b7 once the position supports it.

title: Slav: an early bishop can expose b7
caption: After 7.Qb3: the queen attacks b7 and d5. Early ...Bg4 has created a concrete defensive problem.

comments.8: A risky early bishop sortie in this exact Slav move order. Compare 4...e6 in the analysis variation.
comments.13: The queen attacks both pawns; a generic bishop-out-first rule is inadequate. The game continued ...e6 Qxb7 and Black had to recover from a pawn deficit.

title: A successful attack is not necessarily a sound sacrifice
caption: After 15...Ng4+: White should consider 16.Kh3, not only retreat. The game's 16.Kg1 allowed the attack to flourish.

comments.28: Played, but not recommended: Stockfish favors White after accurate defense. Keep this as a calculation exercise, not a repertoire sacrifice.
comments.30: White to move: 16.Kh3 is the critical defense. The analysis variation is separate from the game, which continued 16.Kg1.

title: Advance: the queen sees h4 too
caption: After 5.Nh4: e7 is empty, so Qd8 can take the undefended knight on h4. Bishop attacks do not override loose pieces.

comments.9: The knight attacks Bf5 but is undefended on the d8-h4 diagonal. 5...Qxh4 wins it; 6.g3 Qe4+ forks king and rook.
